title: Filtering Whisky Before Bottling | Craft Beer School
desc: Coarse filtration, chill filtration or none: what each removes from whisky, what it costs in texture and how to choose for your release.
teaser: Every whisky gets filtered somehow. The question is how hard you go and what you lose doing it.
standfirst: Before bottling, whisky passes through some kind of filter. At the gentle end it only catches char and splinters. At the other it is chilled and filtered to stop haze. Each step changes how the whisky looks. Some argue it changes how it feels in the mouth.
sections:
Spirit drawn from a cask carries charcoal flakes from the charred inside, wood fragments and sometimes sediment. Nobody wants those in a bottle. At minimum, distilleries pass whisky through a coarse screen or filter to remove visible particles. This step does little to flavour and is close to universal.

The real choice is what happens after that. Our guide to chill filtration and caramel colouring covers the drinker's view. This guide is the producer's.

Whisky contains long chain fatty acid esters and other compounds that stay dissolved at cask strength and room temperature. When whisky is reduced below about 46% ABV and then chilled, some of these come out of solution and form a haze. In a warm bar it may clear again. In a cold shop or with ice, it looks cloudy.

Chill filtration cools the whisky, typically to around 0 °C or a little below, so those compounds come out of solution. The cold whisky then passes through sheet or cartridge filters that catch them. What reaches the bottle stays clear when cold.

Chill filtration gives a bright, stable product that never alarms a customer. Critics argue that the compounds removed also carry some texture and flavour, so the whisky tastes thinner. How big that effect is depends on the whisky, the temperature and the filter. Tasters disagree on it.

What is not in dispute is the market signal. Many enthusiasts look for non chill-filtered on a label and see 46% ABV or higher as a mark of care. A mass market whisky sold over ice may need to stay clear. Decide based on who drinks your whisky and how they serve it.

Most craft distilleries end up on one of these:

  • Coarse filtration only, bottled at 46% or higher. Usually stays clear at normal temperatures. Popular for single malts aimed at enthusiasts.
  • Coarse filtration only, bottled at 40 to 43%. Risk of haze when cold. Some accept it and explain it on the label.
  • Chill filtration, bottled at 40 to 43%. Clear in the cold. Common for blends and products served with ice or water.

There are middle routes too, such as filtering at cool cellar temperature rather than near freezing, which removes some haze-forming material while taking out less. Test before you commit.

Plate and frame filters with cellulose sheets are common in small distilleries. Cartridge housings are simpler to run. Whatever the kit, the grade of filter and the temperature do most of the work. Finer grades and colder whisky remove more.

The floor detail we would insist on: rinse new filter sheets or cartridges with water and then a little of the whisky before collecting product. Send the first run back. New sheets can give a papery taint to the first litres that pass through. Hold the whisky at a steady temperature during the run too, because haze that comes out of solution after filtering ends up in the bottle.
Test for haze before you choose

Take the reduced whisky, hold samples in clean clear bottles in a fridge at around 4 °C overnight and check them against a light. Repeat with samples taken after your chosen filtration. Compare with an unfiltered control. If the unfiltered sample stays bright at your bottling strength, you may not need chill filtration at all.

Indian distribution adds its own test. A bottle can travel in a hot truck, sit in a warm shop, then go into an air-conditioned bar or onto ice. Run a warm and cold cycle on samples as part of your stability testing before release.
Make the decision once and record it

Write the filtration method into the product specification: filter type and grade, temperature, flow and the haze test result. Changing it later changes the product. Drinkers notice. Pair it with your reduction to bottling strength plan, because the two decisions depend on each other.

Filtration is a small step with a big influence on what the customer sees first. Understanding the chemistry behind haze is what lets you choose on purpose instead of copying a neighbour.

Your first step: put two samples of your reduced whisky in the fridge tonight, one filtered and one not. Look at them under a torch in the morning.
faqs: It cools whisky to around 0 °C or a little below so fatty acid esters and similar compounds come out of solution, then filters them out so the whisky stays clear when cold.
Why are many non chill-filtered whiskies bottled at 46%?
At about 46% ABV and above, the compounds that cause cold haze tend to stay dissolved, so the whisky stays clear without chill filtration.
Does chill filtration change the flavour?
Some tasters say it thins texture and flavour. Others notice little difference. The effect depends on the whisky and the filtration conditions.
Not necessarily. Haze from fatty acid esters in non chill-filtered whisky is harmless and often clears when the whisky warms up.
